name: Calcium
lead: Calcium (symbol Ca, atomic number 20) is an alkaline earth metal that is the most abundant metal in the human body and an essential mineral [1][2]. More than 99 percent of body calcium is stored in the skeleton, mostly as hydroxyapatite, where it provides rigidity and acts as a reservoir; the remaining 1 percent in blood and tissues is involved in blood clotting, muscle contraction, nerve transmission, hormone secretion and enzyme activation [2][1]. Dietary calcium comes from dairy products, fortified foods, some leafy greens and supplements.

In bone and appearance-related discussion, calcium is raised as a building block for the skeleton, often together with vitamin D, vitamin K2 and magnesium. Supplementation research has focused on bone density and fracture prevention in older adults and postmenopausal women. Meta-analyses report small increases in bone mineral density from higher calcium intake, while evidence that calcium or vitamin D supplements prevent fractures in community-dwelling older adults has been mixed [6][5][8][3].

No published study has tested calcium supplementation for changing facial or jaw bone structure in healthy adults. Excess intake from supplements can cause hypercalcaemia, and calcium products can interact with some medicines [29].

paras: Calcium and vitamin D supplementation is widely used in osteoporosis management, usually alongside antiresorptive or anabolic drugs [3][16]. Calcium salts have specific medical roles: calcium acetate is a phosphate binder indicated to lower serum phosphorus in end-stage renal disease [29]; intravenous calcium gluconate is used for conditions such as hypocalcaemia and has been tested in obstetric and thyroid-surgery settings [12][27][28]; and intravenous calcium is among therapies evaluated for hyperkalaemia [4].

Calcium appears in bone-health supplement stacks on the reasoning that adequate intake supports bone mineralisation and peak bone mass. This applies to the skeleton in general; no trial has examined whether extra calcium in people who already meet their needs changes facial bone or jaw structure.

A 2015 BMJ meta-analysis of 59 randomised trials in people over 50 found that increasing calcium intake from food raised bone mineral density by about 0.6 to 1.0 percent at the total hip and total body at one year and by 0.7 to 1.8 percent at several sites at two years, with no effect at the forearm; calcium supplements raised density by 0.7 to 1.8 percent at all five sites, with later gains similar in size to those at one year [6]. A 2020 meta-analysis of randomised trials in postmenopausal women found that combined calcium and vitamin D significantly increased total, lumbar-spine, arm and femoral-neck density and reduced hip fracture incidence (relative risk 0.864), with the femoral-neck effect seen only at vitamin D intakes of no more than 400 IU per day [8].

For fractures, a 2017 JAMA meta-analysis of trials in community-dwelling adults over 50 examined calcium, vitamin D and combined supplements against placebo or no treatment and reported no association with lower fracture incidence [5]. A 2026 BMJ systematic review of 69 trials with 153,902 participants re-examined the effect of calcium, vitamin D or both on fractures and falls in adults not receiving osteoporosis drugs [3]. A 2021 review of food-matrix effects describes how absorption differs between dairy, plant foods and supplements, and an older trial described reduced calcium absorption from whole-wheat products [15][13]. A trial in breastfeeding mothers with low calcium intake found that a 1,000 mg daily supplement did not alter breast milk calcium or lactation-related bone changes in the spine, radius or total body [10].

The human literature on calcium is large. Systematic reviews address bone density [6][8] and fractures and falls [5][3], and a narrative review places calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2 and magnesium together in skeletal health [3]. Other randomised or controlled work covers urate lowering with calcium supplementation [11], calcium requirements during lactation [10], absorption from foods [13][15], preoperative calcitriol to prevent hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy [9], intravenous calcium gluconate to reduce uterine atony at caesarean delivery [12], and calcium silicate or calcium-based dental materials in endodontics [7][14].

Registered trials include calcium effects on weight, blood pressure, insulin resistance and postprandial vascular function [19][20][22], women's vascular health with calcium and osteoporosis [23], calcium gluconate for ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome [21][25], empiric calcium in massive transfusion [24], and calcium electroporation in oesophageal cancer [26]. None of the cited studies addresses facial or jaw bone for appearance.

Excess calcium from supplements can cause constipation, kidney stones and hypercalcaemia, and some studies have raised questions about cardiovascular effects of high-dose supplements; clinical guidance generally prefers meeting needs from food where possible. Calcium can also interact with some antibiotics and with thyroid medicines. Prolonged hypercalcaemia from medical disorders can lead to calcification of soft tissue such as arteries. Calcification of coronary arteries is measured by CT calcium scoring in cardiac assessment [17].

Calcium is deposited in bone as hydroxyapatite, while calcium ions act as an intracellular second messenger in signal transduction, in neurotransmitter release and in contraction of all muscle cell types [1][2][18]. Serum calcium is tightly regulated by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D and calcitonin, with bone acting as a reservoir [2]. Calcium acetate, as a drug, binds dietary phosphate in the gut to form an insoluble complex excreted in the stool [29].

Elemental calcium is a soft, silvery-white metal that is never found uncombined in nature; it occurs in limestone (calcium carbonate), gypsum and apatite and is the fifth most abundant element in the Earth's crust [2]. Its most common isotope, 40Ca, makes up about 96.9 percent of natural calcium [1].

Some calcium compounds were known to the ancients, though their chemistry was not understood until the seventeenth century; the metal was isolated in 1808 by Humphry Davy through electrolysis of its oxide, and he named the element [1].

Calcium is among the most common supplements and is also an industrial material used in cement, steelmaking and paper [1]. In physique and bodybuilding forums it is usually mentioned as an electrolyte important to muscle and nerve function, or as a value in blood-test threads, rather than as a looksmaxxing intervention.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, calcium is discussed as a raw material for bone mass, usually alongside vitamin D3, K2 and magnesium, with users asking how to obtain enough of it and which sources to use [30][31][32][33][34].

claims.claim: Adequate calcium is needed to gain bone mass or density
claims.believers: A looksmax.org user asks how to get enough calcium to make any small gains in bone mass or density, and another thread is titled "basic principle of calcium for bones" [30][33].
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report small increases in bone mineral density from higher calcium intake, while evidence that calcium or vitamin D supplements prevent fractures in community-dwelling older adults is mixed; no published study has tested calcium for changing facial or jaw bone in healthy adults [6][5][8][3].

claims.claim: Calcium supplements increase heart attack risk, so food sources are preferable
claims.believers: The same user says calcium supplements increase the risk of heart attacks and that he already eats a lot of red meat and butter [30].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page focus on bone outcomes and report that excess intake from supplements can cause hypercalcaemia; they do not assess cardiovascular risk from calcium supplements [29][3].

claims.claim: Milk has estrogenic effects and can lower testosterone
claims.believers: The user asks whether milk, despite its reputation for calcium, has estrogenic effects that can lower testosterone, and whether zinc and magnesium are also needed for testosterone [30].
claims.experts: The sources cited on this page describe dairy as a dietary calcium source and do not report studies on milk and testosterone [1][2].

claims.claim: Eggshells are a free source of calcium
claims.believers: Two looksmax.org threads, titled "eggshells free calcium you npcs throw away" and one stating that three eggshells provide triple an adult's recommended calcium, promote eggshells as a calcium source [31][32].
claims.experts: Reviews describe calcium absorption as depending on the food matrix and source; the sources cited on this page do not evaluate eggshell calcium [15].

claims.claim: Calcium with D3 and K2 maximises height growth
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread is titled "the role of calcium vitamin d3 and vitamin k2 in maximizing height growth" [34].
claims.experts: Supplementation research cited here concerns bone density and fracture prevention in older adults and postmenopausal women, not height in healthy people [3][5][8].
